concepts.def: Tension is a pulling force that stretches a member; compression is a pushing force that squashes it; most structures carry both.
A strut is a structural member that resists compression, while a tie resists tension, as in the diagonal members of bridges and roofs.
Adding diagonal members to frames to form triangles, the only polygon that cannot change shape without changing the length of a side.
A horizontal member spanning a gap; under a central load a simply supported beam bends, with its top in compression and bottom in tension.
Static loads are constant, like a building's own weight; dynamic loads change or move, like wind, traffic or people walking.
A structure's resistance to toppling, improved by a wide base, a low centre of gravity and firm anchorage to the ground.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Structures — a core area of GCSE Design Technology.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Structures brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Structures.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Why does triangulation make a frame rigid?
options: A triangle cannot change shape without changing a side length
Triangles contain more material than squares
Triangles weigh less than any other shape
Triangles look more attractive

mcqs.q: Which structural member is designed to resist tension?
options: A tie
A strut
A foundation
A gusset plate

mcqs.q: In a simply supported beam loaded at its centre, where is the compression?
options: Along the top surface
Along the bottom surface
Only at the supports
Evenly through the whole beam

mcqs.q: Which change makes a free-standing structure more stable?
options: Lowering its centre of gravity and widening its base
Raising its centre of gravity
Narrowing its base
Making it taller without anchorage

mcqs.q: Why are triangles used in structures instead of rectangles?
options: Triangles are stronger because they contain more material than other shapes.
Triangles are used because they are the cheapest shape to paint.
A triangle cannot change shape without changing the length of a side, so it is inherently rigid; a rectangle can rack sideways into a parallelogram unless braced.
A strut is the horizontal floor panel of a structure.

mcqs.q: Where do tension and compression occur in a loaded beam?
options: Triangles are used because they are the cheapest shape to paint.
In a simply supported beam bending under a central load, the top surface is in compression and the bottom surface is in tension, with a neutral axis between.
The whole beam is in tension when a load is applied.
Tension only occurs at the two supports of the beam.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between a strut and a tie?
options: Strut and tie are interchangeable names for any structural member.
A strut carries compression and must resist buckling; a tie carries tension and can even be a cable, since pulling forces keep it taut.
Triangles are used because they are the cheapest shape to paint.
A strut is the horizontal floor panel of a structure.
